problem: The plotted mild-steel curve makes the straight-line elastic part run up to about 400 MPa and puts yield near 415–430 MPa, while standard values for mild steel are a proportional limit near 200 MPa and a yield point near 250 MPa. The strain axis also stops at 8×10⁻³, so fracture appears at about 0.7 % strain. That is brittle behaviour and contradicts the text, which says mild steel is ductile with a long plastic region. A student reading the numbers off the axes will get wrong values for yield stress and fracture strain.
fix: End the straight line near 200 MPa and show yield near 250 MPa. Show the plastic and necking part with a broken (not-to-scale) strain axis, labelled as such, because mild steel breaks at strains of order 0.2 (20 %), not 0.008. Change the caption to read: stress rises linearly to roughly 200 MPa (the proportional limit), bends near the yield point around 250 MPa, then the plastic and necking part is drawn with a break in the strain axis.

problem: The Hooke line is drawn all the way to 600 MPa, far past the proportional limit, without a label saying it is only an extension of the elastic line.
fix: Draw the Hooke line only through the elastic region, or dash it beyond the proportional limit and label it 'extension of the elastic line (Hooke's law does not hold here)'.

problem: The text says some books write σ for Poisson's ratio, but σ was defined two lines earlier as stress and is used again in the bulk-modulus formula. Students will read σ as stress everywhere.
fix: Write: Poisson's ratio ν = lateral strain ÷ longitudinal strain; some books use the symbol µ for it. In this book σ always means stress.

problem: The trap says writing strain in m/m loses marks. m/m equals 1, so it is a harmless way to show strain is dimensionless; only N/m² is genuinely wrong for strain. As written, a student may think m/m is an error.
fix: Write: strain is a pure ratio with no units; m/m is acceptable because it equals 1, but N/m² is a stress unit and wrong for strain.
